chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
title: The Savoy battle with Benny Goodman
summary: A tall substitute drummer broke up the house on "By Heck", then Chick sat in for "King Porter Stomp" to open the battle, after the band changed tempos to fool Goodman.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: I recall you mentioning Big Sid playing and Bill Beeson substituting for Chick Webb.

There was a one drummer I'm going to tell you about. You have to add that in. I can't think of his name now. He was the drummer -- a real tall fella. He was the drummer that played the night we played with Benny Goodman. you understand that (inaudible). Benny asked us to change bandstands if he came up to play against us, you know. Because that was the Benny Goodman (inaudible), you know.
Savoy, yeah. And Chick say, "Okay, we'll change. We'll sit over. You take our number one bandstand, we'll take the number two. It don't make no difference to us," you know.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

"Be our guest." So, the place was packed, you know, way before the band leader started (inaudible). I think the Savoy Sultan was just entertaining (inaudible). And we came on and played the first set. Chick didn't play the first set with us that night. We played a set, and in this set had one of Chick's favorite little drum things. He like to play "Bye Heck." I'm talking to uh -- sorry, I couldn't give you the fella's name, because I was talking to Dick Vance last night about some information that I wanted to talk to you about. And we did this particular number, "Bye Heck." And I used to play the bass saxophone and the brakes on it. And some time Chick -- It was written for Chick, see. Chick used to play it. So that night, we let this fella sit in to play the drums -- a real tall fella. Real wild, real crazy, you know.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
And he played -- we played (inaudible). When we got down to playing By Heck, he broke up the Savoy Ballroom with his brakes.

Because he, you know, he was watching -- he was another fella that stayed 'round Chick Webb all the time. He learned a lot from Chick. He did all of Chick's brakes near as he could, you know. And the place just went wild, you know. Right after that -- that was the last number on that set.

Then Benny Goodman came over and crossed over -- the crowd was so big -- because he had to get up on our side and walk to the other bandstand. Chick came over just behind him when he (inaudible) sat down. And Benny got set up, started over and sat down.
Well, we hadn't finished the set. Chick sat down behind the drums and we played "King Porter Stomp."
That was opening up the battle. Chick down and said, "King Porter Stomp."

get it on. That was the (Inaudible) battle with Benny Goodman. It was a very funny thing. Benny used to come to the Savoy all the time to listen to Chick play, you know. Couple of weeks before the battle, we say, "Hey, Benny's in the house." (Inaudible), "Okay." What we would do, we would change the tempo of the thing so he wouldn't know what tempo we were going to play different numbers. If it was fast, we would drop it down a little bit. We changed all the sets we're going to play. We changed the tempos, you know. (Inaudible), you know. And the night when he came up to hear us play, we would go back to the original tempos, you know. "Clap Hands" was If (Inaudible) one tempo, well we'd drop it down. The night we're going to play we live it up a little bit, you know. Real sensational, you know -- things like that.
